meta.tagline: A deduction card game for scientists: find the flaw hidden in the manuscript before your review rounds run out.

question.name: Question
question.ask: What the study set out to answer, and what was planned.

method.name: Method
method.ask: How the study was designed and run.

sample.name: Sample
sample.ask: Who or what was studied, and who was lost.

measurement.name: Measurement
measurement.ask: How the outcomes and exposures were measured.

analysis.name: Analysis
analysis.ask: How the data were analysed and turned into a conclusion.

accept.name: Accept
accept.when: No flaw: every request was answered well.

minor.name: Minor revisions
minor.short: A gap in the reporting or the wording. The conclusion stands.
minor.when: Fix with clearer reporting or softer claims; no new analysis.

major.name: Major revisions
major.short: A real problem that the authors can still fix.
major.when: Fix with new analyses, data the authors already hold, or a redone step.

reject.name: Reject
reject.short: A fatal flaw. Only a new study could answer the question.
reject.when: The data themselves are compromised; no reanalysis can rescue them.

registration.name: Registration
registration.ask: Show the registry entry or protocol: what was planned, and when it was registered.

hypothesis.name: Prespecified aims
hypothesis.ask: State the objectives or hypotheses as they were set before the data came in.

allocation.name: Randomisation
allocation.ask: How was the allocation sequence made, and who could see it before each assignment?

intervention.name: Intervention details
intervention.ask: Describe the intervention and the comparator well enough for someone to repeat them.

timeline.name: Setting and dates
timeline.ask: When and where were exposures, outcomes and follow-up measured?

search.name: Search strategy
search.ask: List every source you searched and give the full search strings.

reflexivity.name: Reflexivity
reflexivity.ask: Who collected the data, and what was their relationship with the participants?

reference-standard.name: Reference standard
reference-standard.ask: Which test decided who truly had the condition, and did everyone get it?

recruitment.name: Recruitment
recruitment.ask: Who was eligible, and how were participants found and selected?

flow.name: Flow diagram
flow.ask: How many were eligible, included, lost and analysed, and why was anyone lost?

sample-size.name: Sample size
sample-size.ask: How was the number of participants decided?

saturation.name: Data saturation
saturation.ask: When did you stop collecting data, and how did you judge it was enough?

blinding.name: Blinding
blinding.ask: Who knew the groups, or the other test results, when the outcomes were assessed?

instrument.name: Measures
instrument.ask: How exactly was each outcome and exposure measured, and is the measure valid?

coding.name: Coding tree
coding.ask: How many people coded the data, and what does the coding tree look like?

risk-of-bias.name: Risk-of-bias assessment
risk-of-bias.ask: How was the risk of bias in each included study judged, and by whom?

missing-data.name: Missing data
missing-data.ask: How much data was missing, and how was it handled?

sensitivity.name: Sensitivity analysis
sensitivity.ask: Do the results hold under other reasonable analysis choices?

confounding.name: Confounder adjustment
confounding.ask: Which confounders were adjusted for, and why those?

analysis-set.name: Analysis set
analysis-set.ask: Who or what was counted in each analysis, and in which group?

themes.name: Theme derivation
themes.ask: Were the themes set in advance, or derived from the data?

thresholds.name: Test cut-offs
thresholds.ask: Was the cut-off for a positive test fixed before the data, or chosen after?

heterogeneity.name: Heterogeneity
heterogeneity.ask: How much did the studies' results differ, and was that explored?

reporting-bias.name: Reporting bias
reporting-bias.ask: Could missing studies or missing results have biased the pooled estimate?

switched-registration.name: Switched after registration
switched-registration.short: What the paper reports is not what was registered, and the change is not explained.

harking.name: HARKing
harking.short: A hypothesis written after the results, presented as if it came first.

p-hacking.name: p-hacking
p-hacking.short: Many analyses tried, and only the one that reached significance reported.

overclaiming.name: Overclaiming
overclaiming.short: The conclusion claims more than the design can show.

predictable-allocation.name: Predictable allocation
predictable-allocation.short: Whoever enrols participants can foresee or steer the next assignment.

reverse-timing.name: Exposure after outcome
reverse-timing.short: The 'cause' was measured or counted after the outcome had begun.

insider-interviewer.name: Interviewer with power
insider-interviewer.short: The person collecting the data has power over the participants.

verification-bias.name: Partial verification
verification-bias.short: Only some participants got the reference standard, chosen by their test result.

narrow-search.name: Narrow search
narrow-search.short: Too few sources searched, so relevant studies are missed.

hand-picked.name: Hand-picked participants
hand-picked.short: Staff chose who took part by unwritten criteria, so results may not carry over.

attrition.name: Selective loss to follow-up
attrition.short: The people lost differ from those who stayed, in ways that matter.

control-selection.name: Unsuitable controls
control-selection.short: Controls do not come from the population that produced the cases.

volunteer-sample.name: Self-selected sample
volunteer-sample.short: Whoever chose to answer, so the sample can't stand for the population.

early-saturation.name: Saturation not reached
early-saturation.short: Data collection stopped for practical reasons, yet saturation is claimed.

spectrum-bias.name: Spectrum bias
spectrum-bias.short: Clear-cut cases compared with healthy people, leaving out the hard cases.

publication-bias.name: Unpublished studies left out
publication-bias.short: Only published studies count, and those lean towards positive results.

unreported-exclusions.name: Unreported exclusions
unreported-exclusions.short: Animals or participants dropped from the analysis without a word.

unblinded-assessors.name: Unblinded assessors
unblinded-assessors.short: The people judging the outcome knew who got what.

recall-bias.name: Recall bias
recall-bias.short: Cases and controls remember past exposures differently.

unvalidated-measure.name: Unvalidated measure
unvalidated-measure.short: A home-made measure with no evidence that it captures what it claims.

single-coder.name: Single coder, no audit trail
single-coder.short: One person coded everything, and nobody can follow how.

review-bias.name: Unblinded test reading
review-bias.short: The test was read by someone who already knew the right answer.

no-risk-of-bias.name: No risk-of-bias assessment
no-risk-of-bias.short: Included studies were never judged for bias.

per-protocol.name: Per-protocol only
per-protocol.short: Only participants who stuck to the plan were analysed.

confounding.name: Uncontrolled confounding
confounding.short: A factor behind both exposure and outcome was left unadjusted.

missing-data.name: Missing data ignored
missing-data.short: Incomplete records dropped, although who is missing is not random.

themes-from-guide.name: Themes = interview questions
themes-from-guide.short: The 'themes' are the headings of the interview guide.

data-driven-cutoff.name: Data-driven cut-off
data-driven-cutoff.short: The cut-off was tuned on the same data used to judge accuracy.

unexplored-heterogeneity.name: Unexplored heterogeneity
unexplored-heterogeneity.short: Studies disagree strongly, yet one pooled number is presented as the answer.

pseudoreplication.name: Pseudoreplication
pseudoreplication.short: Repeated measurements of one unit counted as independent units.

S1.title: Back on track
S1.claim: A 12-week supervised exercise programme improves physical function in adults with chronic low back pain.

question.submitted: Does a 12-week exercise programme improve function in chronic low back pain, compared with usual care?

registration.sound: Registered before the first patient, with function at 12 weeks as primary outcome, as in the paper.
registration.flaw: Registered with pain at 12 weeks as primary outcome. The paper makes function primary and never says why.
registration.why: Switching the primary outcome after seeing the data lets a chance finding pass as the main result. Fixable: report the registered outcome as primary and explain the change.

hypothesis.sound: Hypothesis stated: the programme improves the function score by at least 3 points more than usual care.

method.submitted: Randomised trial in four clinics; patients allocated 1:1 to supervised exercise or usual care.

allocation.sound: Computer-made sequence in random blocks, released by a central web service only after enrolment.
allocation.flaw: Patients seen on Mondays and Wednesdays got exercise; patients seen on other days got usual care.
allocation.why: Staff could foresee each allocation and steer who was enrolled on which day, so the groups may differ from the start. No reanalysis can undo that.

intervention.sound: Two supervised sessions a week for 12 weeks; the full exercise protocol is in a supplement.

sample.submitted: 240 adults with low back pain for more than 3 months, referred by their GPs.

recruitment.sound: All consecutive referrals screened against published criteria; 240 of 412 eligible and consenting.
recruitment.flaw: Physiotherapists enrolled only patients they judged 'motivated to exercise'; no written criteria.
recruitment.why: Randomisation still balances the groups, so the comparison is fair, but the result may not apply to typical patients. Minor: report it and narrow the claims.

flow.sound: Flow diagram: 412 screened, 240 randomised, 226 analysed; losses similar per arm, with reasons.

measurement.submitted: Function scored with a standard performance test at 12 weeks.

blinding.sound: Tests scored by assessors from another clinic who did not know anyone's group.
blinding.flaw: Each patient's own physiotherapist scored the test, knowing who had the exercise programme.
blinding.why: Assessors who know the groups tend to see the effect they expect. A 12-week performance test can't be repeated blind afterwards, so the main result can't be rescued.

instrument.sound: The performance test has published reliability and validity in low back pain.

analysis.submitted: Groups compared with a linear model adjusted for baseline function.

missing-data.sound: 6% of outcomes missing, handled by multiple imputation; complete-case results agree.

analysis-set.sound: Every randomised patient analysed in the group they were assigned to.
analysis-set.flaw: Only patients who attended at least 80% of sessions were analysed: 61 of 120 in the exercise arm.
analysis-set.why: Dropping non-adherers breaks randomisation: people who keep exercising differ from those who stop. Fixable: reanalyse everyone as randomised (intention to treat).

S2.title: Late-night scrolling
S2.claim: Heavy social-media use at age 13 predicts sleep problems at age 15.

question.submitted: Does heavy social-media use at age 13 predict sleep problems at age 15?

hypothesis.sound: Hypothesis from the funded proposal, cited: more daily use, more sleep problems at 15, in girls and boys alike.
hypothesis.flaw: The introduction predicts an effect in girls only. The proposal predicted it for everyone; only girls showed it.
hypothesis.why: A hypothesis written after the results makes a chance subgroup finding look like a confirmed prediction. Fixable: restore the original hypothesis and label the girls-only result exploratory.

registration.sound: Not preregistered; the authors say so plainly in the limitations.

method.submitted: Prospective school-based cohort with questionnaires at ages 13 and 15.

timeline.sound: Use measured at 13 and sleep at 15, two years apart, at the same point in the school year.
timeline.flaw: Both were asked at 15: pupils recalled how much they had used social media two years earlier.
timeline.why: Use at 13 is recalled after the sleep problems began, so the timing that made it a prediction is gone. Only data collected at 13 could fix this.

sample.submitted: 3,000 pupils from 40 schools enrolled at 13; 2,310 followed up at 15.

flow.sound: Losses shown by school and reason; leavers and stayers had similar use and sleep at 13.
flow.flaw: Heavy users were twice as likely to be lost by 15; leavers and stayers are never compared.
flow.why: If the heavy users who left slept differently, the estimate is biased. Fixable: compare leavers with stayers and correct with weighting or imputation.

sample-size.sound: Size set by the parent cohort; the paper reports the precision this gives the main estimate.

measurement.submitted: Sleep problems at 15 measured by questionnaire.

instrument.sound: A validated adolescent sleep questionnaire, plus a week of wrist actigraphy in a subsample.
instrument.flaw: One yes/no item written for this study, 'Do you often sleep badly?', with no validation.
instrument.why: One home-made yes/no item can't show it measures sleep problems. Fixable in part: use the cohort's fuller sleep measures, or validate the item in a subsample, and temper the claims.

analysis.submitted: Logistic regression of sleep problems on hours of use, adjusted for confounders.

confounding.sound: Adjusted for sleep, mood and family income at 13, chosen in advance from a causal diagram.

sensitivity.sound: Results hold with use in hours per day and with cut-offs at 2, 3 and 4 hours.
sensitivity.flaw: Use was split at 3 hours after trying cut-offs from 1 to 5; only the one with p < 0.05 is reported.
sensitivity.why: Trying many cut-offs and reporting the one that works inflates false positives. Fixable: analyse hours as a continuous measure, or show every cut-off.

S3.title: Sleeping pills and hip fracture
S3.claim: Benzodiazepine use doubles the risk of hip fracture in people over 70.

question.submitted: Does benzodiazepine use raise the risk of hip fracture in people over 70?

hypothesis.sound: Protocol hypothesis: benzodiazepine use raises hip-fracture risk. The paper tests that one question.
hypothesis.flaw: Nine sleep medicines were tested. The headline is the one significant drug, with no correction for nine tests.
hypothesis.why: With nine tests, one 'significant' result is likely by chance alone. Fixable: report all nine, correct for multiple testing, and call the single-drug finding exploratory.

method.submitted: Case-control study: 400 hip-fracture cases and 800 matched controls from two regions.

timeline.sound: Drug use counted only in the year before each case's fracture date, with the same window for its controls.
timeline.flaw: Drug use counted from 6 months before to 1 month after the fracture, when many start sleeping pills in hospital.
timeline.why: Pills started because of the fracture are counted as its cause. Fixable: rerun the analysis with use before the fracture date only.

sample.submitted: Cases from hospital admissions; controls matched on age and sex.

recruitment.sound: Controls drawn at random from the same regions' population register.
recruitment.flaw: Controls were volunteers recruited at senior fitness clubs.
recruitment.why: Fitness-club members take fewer sleeping pills and fall less than the population the cases came from, so the comparison is biased from the start. New controls are needed.

flow.sound: 81% of cases and 76% of controls took part; reasons for refusal are reported.

measurement.submitted: Benzodiazepine use assessed in the same way for cases and controls.

instrument.sound: Use taken from pharmacy dispensing records for cases and controls alike.
instrument.flaw: Use recalled in interviews: cases on the ward days after their fracture, controls by phone.
instrument.why: Cases search their memory harder, in a different setting, so their use is over-reported. Fixable in part: check the answers against pharmacy records.

blinding.sound: Records abstracted by staff who did not know who was a case.

analysis.submitted: Conditional logistic regression, adjusted for other risk factors.

confounding.sound: Adjusted for dementia, frailty, previous falls and other fall-risk drugs, chosen in advance.
confounding.flaw: Adjusted for age and sex only. Dementia and frailty, which lead to both pills and falls, are ignored.
confounding.why: Frail people get more sleeping pills and fall more, so part of the 'drug effect' may be frailty. Fixable if the data hold these factors: adjust for them and show both estimates.

sensitivity.sound: Results similar when restricted to new users and to fractures from simple falls.

S4.title: Burnout in the doctorate
S4.claim: Almost half of PhD students are burnt out, and poor supervision causes it.

question.submitted: How common is burnout among PhD students, and what is it associated with?

hypothesis.sound: Aims: estimate prevalence and describe associations. The conclusion stays descriptive.
hypothesis.flaw: The aim is descriptive, yet the abstract concludes that poor supervision causes burnout.
hypothesis.why: A one-off survey can't show which came first, burnout or poor supervision. Minor: rewrite the conclusion as an association.

method.submitted: Online survey of PhD students at four universities in spring 2025.

timeline.sound: Survey open for three weeks in March 2025, away from the main submission deadlines.

recruitment.sound: All 2,100 enrolled PhD students were invited by email, with two reminders.
recruitment.flaw: The link was shared on a PhD well-being forum and on social media; anyone could answer.
recruitment.why: Whether people answer depends on how much burnout matters to them, so the prevalence can't be generalised. A new, defined sample is needed.

flow.sound: Numbers who opened, started and finished the survey are reported, with the drop-off at each step.

measurement.submitted: Burnout measured with a questionnaire scored against a cut-off.

instrument.sound: A validated burnout inventory, scored with the manual's published cut-off.
instrument.flaw: Five items written by the authors; 'burnout' means scoring above the midpoint; no validation.
instrument.why: A prevalence is only as good as the measure and its cut-off. Fixable only in part: give validity evidence, or report scores instead of a prevalence.

analysis.submitted: Prevalence with 95% confidence intervals; regression for associations.

missing-data.sound: 3% of items missing, prorated as the scale's manual specifies.
missing-data.flaw: The 22% who skipped any item were dropped; skipping was commonest among those reporting long hours.
missing-data.why: If the students under most pressure skipped items, dropping them biases the prevalence. Fixable: multiple imputation, and compare completers with non-completers.

sensitivity.sound: Estimates weighted by faculty and sex give the same prevalence within 2 points.

S5.title: Moral distress in intensive care
S5.claim: ICU nurses' moral distress centres on staffing, families and end-of-life decisions.

question.submitted: How do intensive-care nurses experience moral distress around end-of-life decisions?

hypothesis.sound: An exploratory aim, stated up front, and no hypothesis, as suits an interview study.

method.submitted: Semi-structured interviews with ICU nurses at one university hospital.

reflexivity.sound: Interviews by a researcher from another hospital with no role over the nurses; her nursing background is described.
reflexivity.flaw: Every interview was done by the unit's head nurse, who also writes the nurses' appraisals.
reflexivity.why: Nurses are unlikely to speak freely to the person who appraises them, so the data themselves are compromised. New interviews are needed.

sample.submitted: Fourteen nurses, chosen for a range of experience and shift patterns.

recruitment.sound: Purposive sampling by years of experience and shift pattern; 3 of 17 nurses approached declined.

saturation.sound: Interviews continued until three in a row added no new codes; the paper shows how this was judged.
saturation.flaw: Data collection stopped at 14 because the project ended. Saturation is claimed but not shown.
saturation.why: Saturation means new data stop adding insight, not that time ran out. Fixable: show how completeness was judged, or add interviews.

measurement.submitted: Interviews audio-recorded, transcribed in full and coded.

coding.sound: Two researchers coded independently and met to settle differences; the coding tree is in a supplement.
coding.flaw: One researcher coded every transcript. There is no coding tree and no second reader.
coding.why: With one coder and no audit trail, readers can't judge how the codes came from the data. Fixable: a second coder, the coding tree and an audit trail.

instrument.sound: The interview guide was piloted with two nurses and is given in full.

analysis.submitted: Reflexive thematic analysis produced four themes.

themes.sound: Themes were built from codes across interviews and checked against the full data set.
themes.flaw: The four themes are the four headings of the interview guide, although the paper says they came from the data.
themes.why: Using the interview questions as themes summarises the guide, not the data; Braun & Clarke (2006) name it a pitfall. Fixable: redo the analysis.

S6.title: A scan for appendicitis
S6.claim: Bedside ultrasound by emergency doctors detects appendicitis in children with 97% sensitivity.

question.submitted: How accurate is bedside ultrasound by emergency doctors for appendicitis in children?

registration.sound: Registered before recruitment, with the same target condition, population and cut-off as the paper.
registration.flaw: Registered for patients of all ages. The paper reports children only and never mentions the adults.
registration.why: Leaving out a registered group can hide results that didn't suit. Fixable: report the whole registered population, or explain why not.

hypothesis.sound: Prespecified target: a sensitivity of at least 90%.

method.submitted: Every child had a scan; the diagnosis was confirmed with a reference standard.

reference-standard.sound: Histology if operated on; otherwise a phone follow-up at 14 days. The same rule for every child.
reference-standard.flaw: Only children with a positive scan had surgery and histology. Negatives went home without follow-up.
reference-standard.why: Missed cases among the negatives are never found, so sensitivity looks too high. Fixable only if follow-up can still be obtained for the negatives.

sample.submitted: Children aged 4 to 16 with abdominal pain, at two emergency departments.

recruitment.sound: Consecutive children with suspected appendicitis, on every shift.
recruitment.flaw: Children with surgically confirmed appendicitis, compared with healthy children from a school check-up.
recruitment.why: Comparing clear cases with healthy children leaves out the hard, look-alike cases, so accuracy is inflated. A new, clinically realistic sample is needed.

flow.sound: Flow diagram: 412 eligible, 398 scanned, 6 without a reference standard, each explained.

measurement.submitted: Each scan read as positive or negative for appendicitis.

blinding.sound: Readers knew only the child's age and symptoms, not the lab results or the final diagnosis.
blinding.flaw: Stored scans were read after surgery, by doctors who knew the histology result.
blinding.why: Readers who know the answer read the scan in its light, which inflates accuracy. Fixable: re-read the stored scans blind.

analysis.submitted: Sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals.

thresholds.sound: Positive meant an appendix wider than 6 mm, a cut-off fixed in the protocol.
thresholds.flaw: The 6 mm cut-off was picked after the data, as the one giving the best accuracy.
thresholds.why: A cut-off tuned on the same data flatters accuracy. Fixable: use a prespecified cut-off, or validate this one in new data.

missing-data.sound: Inconclusive scans (9%) counted as negative, and as positive in a sensitivity analysis.

S7.title: Mindfulness apps for anxiety
S7.claim: Mindfulness apps reduce anxiety in adults, with a moderate pooled effect.

question.submitted: Do mindfulness apps reduce anxiety in adults, compared with control conditions?

registration.sound: Registered on PROSPERO before screening; outcomes and methods match the paper.
registration.flaw: PROSPERO lists depression as the primary outcome. The review leads with anxiety and doesn't say why.
registration.why: Choosing the headline outcome after seeing the results lets the best-looking one win. Fixable: report the registered outcome first and explain the change.

hypothesis.sound: Question in PICO form: adults, app-based mindfulness, any control, anxiety symptoms.

method.submitted: Systematic search for randomised trials, screened by two reviewers.

search.sound: Five databases and two trial registers, no language limits; full search strings in a supplement.
search.flaw: PubMed only, English only, no trial registers; the search string isn't given.
search.why: One database misses many trials, and the missed ones are not a random set. Fixable: redo the search across several sources.

sample.submitted: 23 randomised trials with 4,380 adults were included.

recruitment.sound: Any randomised trial was eligible, published or not, including register results and theses.
recruitment.flaw: Only trials published in journals were eligible; register results and theses were excluded.
recruitment.why: Unpublished trials more often find no effect, so leaving them out inflates the pooled effect. Fixable: widen eligibility and look for them.

flow.sound: PRISMA flow diagram: 1,204 records, 61 full texts, 23 included; every exclusion has a reason.

measurement.submitted: Results and study quality extracted by two reviewers.

risk-of-bias.sound: Two reviewers applied RoB 2 to each trial independently; judgements shown domain by domain.
risk-of-bias.flaw: No risk-of-bias tool was used; trials were called 'high quality' because they were peer-reviewed.
risk-of-bias.why: Without judging each trial's bias, nobody can tell whether the effect rests on weak trials. Fixable: assess with RoB 2 and run a sensitivity analysis by risk of bias.

analysis.submitted: Random-effects meta-analysis of standardised mean differences.

heterogeneity.sound: I² = 34%; a subgroup analysis by type of control was planned and reported.
heterogeneity.flaw: I² = 89%, yet one pooled effect is presented as the answer, and the differences are not explored.
heterogeneity.why: When trials disagree this much, one average may describe none of them. Fixable: explore the causes (subgroups, meta-regression) and temper the summary.

reporting-bias.sound: Funnel plot and Egger's test across the 23 trials show no clear asymmetry.

S8.title: A drug for stroke mice
S8.claim: Compound NR-4, given after a stroke, cuts brain damage in mice by 40%.

question.submitted: Does compound NR-4, given after a stroke, reduce brain damage in mice?

registration.sound: Protocol registered beforehand, with infarct volume at 72 hours as primary outcome, as reported.
registration.flaw: Registered with a 24-hour behaviour score as primary. The paper reports infarct volume and omits the behaviour score.
registration.why: Dropping the registered outcome hides a result that may not have suited. Fixable: report the behaviour score and explain the switch.

hypothesis.sound: Hypothesis stated: NR-4 reduces infarct volume at 72 hours compared with vehicle.

method.submitted: Mice with an induced stroke received NR-4 or vehicle one hour later.

allocation.sound: Computer-made random list, held by a colleague who did no surgery.
allocation.flaw: The first mice taken out of each cage got NR-4; the rest got vehicle.
allocation.why: The mice caught first can differ (calmer, slower, smaller), so the groups may differ before treatment. The experiment has to be repeated with random allocation.

intervention.sound: Dose, route, timing, vehicle and anaesthesia described; the vehicle looked identical.

sample.submitted: Twelve mice per group, as planned.

sample-size.sound: Power calculation from pilot data: 12 per group to detect a 30% reduction.

flow.sound: All 24 mice analysed; no deaths and no exclusions.
flow.flaw: Five NR-4 mice died or were excluded; they were replaced and are not mentioned.
flow.why: Replacing animals that died hides harm and can leave only the mice that responded. Fixable: report every animal and analyse with the losses included.

measurement.submitted: Infarct volume measured on stained brain slices at 72 hours.

blinding.sound: Slices were coded; the person measuring them did not know the groups.
blinding.flaw: The researcher who dosed the mice also measured the slices, knowing each group.
blinding.why: Tracing infarct edges takes judgement that expectations can sway. Fixable here, unlike in a live test: the stored slices can be re-measured blind.

instrument.sound: Infarct volume defined in the methods and corrected for brain swelling.

analysis.submitted: Groups compared with a t-test; p < 0.001.

analysis-set.sound: Each mouse counted once, with its slices averaged: 12 per group.
analysis-set.flaw: Each brain slice counted as a separate observation: 120 slices instead of 24 mice.
analysis-set.why: Slices from one mouse are not independent, so the p-value is far too small. Fixable: reanalyse with the mouse as the unit.
